2027-03-07.title: Fourth Sunday of Lent (Laetare)
readings: The wrath and the mercy of the Lord are shown in the exile and the release of his people
Let my tongue be silenced if I ever forget you!
Dead through our trespasses, by grace you have been saved
God sent his Son into the world so that the world might be saved through him
2027-03-07.alt: Year B. Laetare Sunday: rose vestments may be worn, and the organ and flowers, kept sober during Lent, may be used. Where there are catechumens, the Year A readings may be used every year, and they are always used at a Mass with the Second Scrutiny of the elect: 1 Samuel 16:1b, 6–7, 10–13a; Psalm 23:1–3a, 3b–4, 5, 6 (The Lord is my shepherd; there is nothing I shall want); Ephesians 5:8–14; John 9:1–41 (the man born blind). The memorial of Sts Perpetua and Felicity is not kept this year because it falls on Sunday. No Gloria. Liturgical colour: violet or rose.
2027-03-07.verse: For God so loved the world that he gave his only Son, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but may have eternal life.
theo: The Fourth Sunday of Lent takes its old name from the first word of the Entrance Antiphon: Laetare, “Rejoice, Jerusalem.” We have passed the middle of the forty days, and the Church lets a little of Easter's light shine through. Where it is the custom, the priest wears rose instead of violet, as the sky lightens before dawn. The first reading tells the saddest chapter of Israel's history and turns it into hope. The leaders and people were “exceedingly unfaithful,” and they polluted the house of the LORD. Yet God “sent persistently to them by his messengers, because he had compassion on his people.” They mocked the messengers and scoffed at the prophets, “until… there was no remedy.” Jerusalem was burned, the Temple destroyed, and the survivors carried off to Babylon. The Psalm gives voice to the exiles: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down and there we wept when we remembered Zion.” Their captors asked for a song; they hung their harps on the willows. But the Chronicler does not end in tears. After seventy years, as Jeremiah had foretold, “the LORD stirred up the spirit of King Cyrus of Persia,” a pagan king, to send the people home and rebuild the house of God. The last word of the Hebrew Bible, in the order Jewish tradition keeps, is this invitation: “Let him go up.”

The Gospel is part of Jesus' night conversation with Nicodemus, a Pharisee and leader who came to him in the dark. Jesus recalls a strange story from the wilderness. When the people were bitten by poisonous serpents, God told Moses to make a bronze serpent and set it on a pole, “and whenever a serpent bit someone, that person would look at the serpent of bronze and live.” “And just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that whoever believes in him may have eternal life.” In John's Gospel “lifted up” means two things at once: raised on the cross and exalted in glory. The very sign of our wound becomes the place of our healing. Then come the words many call the Gospel in miniature: “For God so loved the world that he gave his only Son, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but may have eternal life.” God's first word to the world is not condemnation: “God did not send the Son into the world to condemn the world, but in order that the world might be saved through him.” Judgment is what happens when the light comes and we choose: “people loved darkness rather than light because their deeds were evil.” Those who do what is true come to the light. Nicodemus himself, who came by night, will come into the open at the end, bringing a hundred pounds of myrrh and aloes for Jesus' burial.

St Paul tells the same good news in other words: “But God, who is rich in mercy, out of the great love with which he loved us even when we were dead through our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ.” We did not climb out of the grave of sin by ourselves: “For by grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God.” Grace comes first, always. But grace is not idle. Paul goes on: “we are what he has made us, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand to be our way of life.” Our fasting, prayer and almsgiving do not buy God's love; they are the fruit of a love already given. Where the Second Scrutiny is celebrated, the Church today reads the Year A Gospel of the man born blind (John 9), and prays that the elect may be freed from darkness and come to Christ, the light of the world. In both Gospels the movement is the same: from darkness to light, from the bite of the serpent to the healing of the cross, from exile to home. That is why we rejoice in the middle of Lent. The One lifted up draws all people to himself.
conn: The Entrance Antiphon begins with Isaiah 66:10: “Rejoice, Jerusalem.” The same joyful pause comes in Advent on Gaudete Sunday. Rose vestments may be worn on both days.
Cyrus took Babylon in 539 BC and soon allowed exiled peoples to return home. Isaiah 45:1 even calls him the Lord's “anointed.” God works through rulers who do not know him.
Jeremiah foretold seventy years of exile (Jeremiah 25:11; 29:10). The Chronicler sees the land “keeping sabbath” while it lay empty.
Numbers 21:4–9. Centuries later King Hezekiah destroyed it because people had begun to worship it (2 Kings 18:4). The sign was meant to point to God's healing, not to replace him.
A Pharisee and member of the council (John 3:1). He speaks up for Jesus in John 7:50–51 and comes openly with myrrh and aloes to bury him in John 19:39.
Jesus speaks three times in John of being “lifted up” (3:14; 8:28; 12:32). It is the cross, and it is his glorification: “I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.”
altar: The Son lifted up on the cross is made present on the altar. At the elevation we look up at the Host and the Chalice, as the Israelites looked up at the serpent, and we live.
God so loved the world that he gave his only Son. In Holy Communion he still gives him to us, truly, Body and Blood, soul and divinity.
outline: Ask: what does it mean to rejoice in the middle of a time of penance?
Point 1 · By the rivers of Babylon
Sin leads to exile, but God's compassion has the last word.
Point 3 · God so loved the world
Not to condemn but to save.
Judgment is our choice before the light.
A rose vestment in the middle of violet: dawn before the day.
“For God so loved the world that he gave his only Son.”
live: Spend five minutes this week gazing at a crucifix in silence, letting Jesus heal what has bitten you.
Teach it to your children and pray it as a morning offering.
Bring one hidden sin into the light of confession before Holy Week.
Do something joyful with your family today, as a foretaste of Easter, while keeping your Lenten resolutions.
fathers: As those who looked at the bronze serpent did not perish from the serpents' bites, so those who look in faith at the death of Christ are healed from the bites of sin. Death came by the serpent; life comes by the death of Christ, which kills death.
God did not give a servant, or an angel, or an archangel, but his only Son. Think how great is the love that gives what is most precious for those who are ungrateful.
We needed a God made flesh and put to death, that we might live. The serpent's poison was overcome by one lifted up on the wood.
magis: The Word became flesh so that we might know God's love: “God so loved the world.”
The bronze serpent: images in the Old Covenant that pointed to salvation by the incarnate Word.
Christ did not come to judge but to save; judgment is our acceptance or refusal of grace.
Grace: the free and undeserved help God gives us, the source of our justification.
St John Paul II, Dives in Misericordia (1980)
The encyclical on God “rich in mercy” (Ephesians 2:4).
Rite of Christian Initiation of Adults
The Second Scrutiny, with the Gospel of the man born blind.
saints: Prince of Poland and Lithuania (1458–1484), son of King Casimir IV, known for prayer, purity, love of the poor and devotion to Our Lady. He died of tuberculosis at twenty-five and is the patron of Lithuania.
Sts Perpetua and Felicity (7 Mar, not kept this year)

Two young mothers martyred at Carthage in 203: Perpetua, a noblewoman nursing her baby, and Felicity, a slave who gave birth in prison days before. Perpetua's own prison diary survives. They are named in the First Eucharistic Prayer.
8 Mar: St John of God (commemoration). 9 Mar: St Frances of Rome (commemoration). 8–13 Mar: Lenten weekdays of the fourth week. 14 Mar: Fifth Sunday of Lent; Third Scrutiny.
2027-03-07.prayer: O God, who through your Word reconcile the human race to yourself in a wonderful way, grant, we pray, that with prompt devotion and eager faith the Christian people may hasten toward the solemn celebrations to come. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Father rich in mercy, you so loved the world that you gave your only Son. Draw us out of the darkness of sin into the light of Christ lifted up, give the elect the light of faith, and bring us rejoicing to Easter. Amen.

quick: God sent his people home from exile because he had compassion on them.
As Moses lifted up the serpent, the Son of Man is lifted up on the cross for our healing.
God so loved the world that he gave his only Son, not to condemn but to save.
2027-03-07.action: Learn John 3:16 by heart and pray it each morning this week.
2027-03-07.question: Do I prefer the darkness in some area of my life, and what would it take to come to the light?
catechism: Christ came not to condemn but to save.
Grace, the free gift of God.
kidsaint: Two brave young mothers who loved Jesus very much, long ago in Africa. One was a rich lady and the other was a servant, but in prison they became like sisters. They did not stop believing in Jesus, even when it was very hard. Lesson: friends who love Jesus make each other brave.
2027-03-07.special: Fourth Sunday of Lent (Laetare). Rose vestments may be worn. Second Scrutiny of the elect; the Year A readings may be used where there are catechumens.
term: Latin for “rejoice,” the first word of the Entrance Antiphon of the Fourth Sunday of Lent (Isaiah 66:10). A day of quiet joy in the middle of Lent, when rose vestments may be worn.

family.explain: Jesus said: God loves the whole world so much that he gave us his only Son, Jesus. Whoever believes in him will live forever with God. God did not send Jesus to punish the world, but to save it. That is why we can be happy, even in Lent!
family.intention: We pray for people who feel that God is angry with them, that they may know his love.
family.ask: Ask: “Can we all learn John 3:16 by heart this week and say it together at night prayer?”

illus: In a hospital in Kozhikode a young nurse was assigned to an old man who shouted at everyone. One night she found him awake, staring at the small crucifix she wore. He asked why she wore it. She said: because when I am tired and angry I look at it, and I remember that someone loved me when I was not lovable. He was quiet for a long time. The next morning he asked to see a priest. He said: I want to look at that cross too.

pm.open: Father rich in mercy, you so loved the world that you gave your only Son. Draw us into his light. Amen.
share: By the rivers of Babylon… we wept when we remembered Zion (Psalm 137:1). Where do I feel in exile from God?
So must the Son of Man be lifted up (John 3:14). What wound do I need to bring to the cross?
People loved darkness rather than light (John 3:19). What am I keeping in the dark?
pm.resp: Let my tongue be silenced if I ever forget you!
interc: For the elect at their Second Scrutiny, that Christ may open their eyes to the light of faith.
For refugees and exiles who weep far from home, that they may find welcome and a way home.
For those who think they are beyond God's love, that they may look on the cross and live.
For rulers, that like Cyrus they may serve the good of peoples.
For our group, that we may rejoice in God's mercy and live in the light.
pm.close: Father, you did not send your Son to condemn but to save. Make us children of the light. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, today the Church says: Laetare, rejoice! We are halfway through Lent, and the violet is touched with rose, like the sky before dawn. Why rejoice in a season of penance? Because today's readings tell us how much God loves us.

The first reading tells of a people who were exceedingly unfaithful. Yet God sent persistently to them by his messengers, because he had compassion on his people (2 Chronicles 36:15). They mocked his prophets and ended in exile, weeping by the rivers of Babylon. But God did not abandon them. After seventy years he stirred up the spirit of Cyrus, and the word went out: let him go up. God always has a way home for us.

In the Gospel Jesus tells Nicodemus: just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up (John 3:14). In the desert those bitten by serpents looked at the bronze serpent and lived. We, bitten by sin, look at Jesus on the cross and live.

Then the words we should all know by heart: for God so loved the world that he gave his only Son, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but may have eternal life (John 3:16). God did not send the Son to condemn the world, but to save it. If there is judgment, it is because we prefer the darkness. Jesus invites us to come to the light.

St Paul says: God, who is rich in mercy, out of the great love with which he loved us even when we were dead through our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ (Ephesians 2:4–5). By grace you have been saved. It is a gift. And we are created in Christ Jesus for good works. Our Lenten works do not buy God's love; they answer it.

So let us rejoice today. Let us look at the cross and live. Let us bring our hidden sins into the light of confession. And let us pray for the elect, who today ask the Lord to open their eyes, so that at Easter they may see. Amen.
kids: Children, today is called Laetare Sunday, rejoice Sunday! Why? Because God loves us so much that he gave us Jesus. Let us learn this verse: God so loved the world that he gave his only Son.
When the people in the desert were bitten by snakes, they looked at the bronze snake and got better. When we are sad or have done wrong, we can look at Jesus on the cross and he makes us better.

intro: Theme: “For God so loved the world that he gave his only Son.”
Exile and homecoming, the serpent lifted up, the love that saves, and the mercy that makes us alive.

q: The LORD, the God of their ancestors, sent persistently to them by his messengers, because he had compassion on his people and on his dwelling place;
But God proves his love for us in that while we still were sinners Christ died for us.
points.apply: Name one area of your life where you feel in exile from God, and bring it to him in prayer this week.

sub: The cross as the place of healing.
q: And the LORD said to Moses, “Make a poisonous serpent, and set it on a pole; and everyone who is bitten shall look at it and live.”
And just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that whoever believes in him may have eternal life.
points.apply: Spend five minutes before a crucifix each day this week, looking and letting yourself be healed.

sub: Not to condemn but to save.
q: Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked, says the Lord GOD, and not rather that they should turn from their ways and live?

For God so loved the world that he gave his only Son, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but may have eternal life. Indeed, God did not send the Son into the world to condemn the world, but in order that the world might be saved through him.
points.apply: Bring one hidden thing into the light of confession before Holy Week.

q: He does not deal with us according to our sins, nor repay us according to our iniquities. For as the heavens are high above the earth, so great is his steadfast love toward those who fear him;
For we are what he has made us, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand to be our way of life.
points.apply: Do one good work this week as a thank-you to God, not as a payment.

concl: God's compassion has the last word over our exile.
Christ lifted up on the cross is the love of God that saves, heals and makes us alive.
2027-03-07.resolve: Learn John 3:16 by heart and pray it every morning until Easter.
